unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! In this unit you use English to talk about maths in real life. You count and name big numbers, all the way up to one million. You learn the words addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. You measure the size, height, weight and distance of things around you, using words like metre and centimetre. You also hunt for straight lines and repeating patterns. Maths is everywhere: in the market, in the kitchen and on the way to school. By the end you will solve a number puzzle, just like Amal and Sami do in this unit's story.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary section. Learn a few maths words each day.
Work through the six grammar lessons, which cover all eight patterns from the source.
Read the story “The Mystery of the Million Shells” and answer the comprehension questions.
Work through the four skills: Reading and listening → Speaking → Writing → Activities.
Finish with the quiz and the self-assessment to see what you have learned.

readings.title: Maths Is Everywhere
readings.setting: A coastal primary school, a home and a market
readings.passageScript:
Numbers are all around us, every single day. Amal notices them first thing in the morning, when she counts the eggs in the basket for breakfast. Later, she walks with her mother to the busy coastal market to buy food for the week.

At the market, stalls are piled high with mangoes, dates and bags of flour. Amal helps her mother add up the prices of everything they buy. She uses addition to find the total, item by item, until every coin is counted.

Back at home, Amal's mother pours a large bowl of sweet dates onto the table. Four cousins have come to visit for the afternoon, and everyone wants a fair share. Amal and her mother use division to split the dates equally, so each cousin gets exactly the same amount.

Before she puts the flour away, Amal measures the size of the flour bag and checks its weight on the kitchen scales. She writes both numbers in her notebook, next to the date.

When it is time to walk her cousins back to their house, Amal counts her steps one by one. She wants to know the distance from her door to theirs. By the time she is home again, she has used addition, division and measuring — all before dinner.

Maths is not only a subject in a book. It is a tool we use every day, at the market, in the kitchen and on the road home.

readings.title: The Mystery of the Million Shells
readings.setting: A coastal primary school, a home and a market
readings.passageScript:
It was a hot afternoon in Cape Coast. The sea breeze blew through the windows of Class 3B.
“Today,” said Teacher Yasmin, “we have a challenge!” The board read: “Can you find the right pattern to solve the number puzzle?” The class clapped.
Sami looked at the table. There were seashells, string, rulers and bowls. “Each team will measure the size, weight and distance between the shells,” said Teacher Yasmin. “Use your eyes, your hands and your maths.”
“What is the first step?” asked Amal.
“Measure the height of your tallest shell,” said the teacher.
Sami's team got to work. “This is a straight shell,” said Amal. “That one is curved.”
“This shell is 2 metres from the bowl,” said Sami. “Let's write that down,” said Amal. The teams wrote their numbers in their books:
Height: 8 cm. Distance: 2 metres. Weight: 150 grams.
“Let's do some addition and subtraction,” said Sami. Amal smiled. “And don't forget multiplication and division!”
Suddenly, Amal pointed at the board. “There's a clue!” she shouted. It read: “There are more than 300 shells. Fewer than a million. Use a pattern. Count carefully.”
Sami counted the shells in one bowl. “There are 25 in this one. And there are 10 bowls.”
“25 times 10 is …?” Amal asked. “Multiplication!” said Sami. “That's 250.”
“And what if we add the shells on the table?” Amal asked. Sami replied, “Then it is over 300. Maybe 400.” “Still far from a million,” Amal laughed.
“Can you measure this shell?” Sami asked. “I can't,” Amal said. “It is too small, and the line isn't straight.” “Use the other ruler,” said Sami. “It has better units.” “Good idea,” Amal said. “I will do it now.”
Teacher Yasmin walked by. “These numbers are correct. But remember, maths is not only about numbers. It is about facts and smart thinking.”
“Shall we check our pattern again?” Amal asked. “Yes,” said Sami. “Let's see if our division is equal.”
Later that day, each team shared their answers. Amal stood up and said: “We used multiplication and addition. We counted by fives. We measured distance in metres and height in centimetres. Our total number of shells is 375.”
Teacher Yasmin smiled. “You all did well. The answer is … 375 shells. Amal's team found the right pattern.” The class clapped.
Sami whispered, “Teamwork is good because we learn more together.”
The teacher gave a final task. “Write a report using these words: number, measure, pattern, distance. Add one new maths fact.” Sami wrote: “We measured the distance from the bowl. We found a pattern in the numbers. One fact I learned: 25 × 10 = 250.”
As they packed up, Amal said, “I've got a new idea for next week. Let's count the school chairs.” Sami laughed. “Only if we stop before a million!”

grammar.title: Present Simple and Imperatives
grammar.explanation: The Present Simple tells about things that happen often or facts that are always true, like “The sun rises in the east.” An imperative is a command or instruction, like “Measure the height.” Both help us speak and write clearly, especially in maths.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present Simple: subject + verb (add s for he, she, it). “I count the shells.” / “She counts the shells.”
Imperative: just the verb, with no subject. “Count the numbers.” / “Measure the table.”
Negative imperative: use Don't. “Don't run in the hall.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “He measure the desk.” ✗
Fix: add s for he/she/it: “He measures the desk.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: For an imperative, just say the verb — you are the boss giving one clear order. For he, she, it in Present Simple, don't forget the s!
grammar.practice: ______ (Count) the numbers on the board. (imperative) | She ______ (measure) the rope every morning. (present simple) | ______ (Measure) the height of your desk. (imperative) | We ______ (add) the prices at the market. (present simple) Answer key: 1) Count the numbers on the board. 2) She measures the rope every morning. 3) Measure the height of your desk. 4) We add the prices at the market.

grammar.title: ‘Have got’ for Ownership
grammar.explanation: We use have got to talk about things we own or have. It helps us tell people about our belongings, like “I've got a ruler.”

I / you / we / they have got (’ve got). “We have got ten bowls.”

grammar.title: Can / Can't for Ability

grammar.title: Demonstratives (This / That)
grammar.explanation: This and that point to things. We use this for something near us and that for something farther away. This makes it clear which thing we mean.

grammar.title: Short Future Responses + Question Forms + Cause and Effect with ‘Because’
grammar.explanation: Short future answers agree with I will and refuse with I won't. Questions hunt for information, so we swap the subject and the helping verb. Because joins what happened to the reason why it happened.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Short answers: “I will!” to agree; “I won't.” to refuse. Other subjects work too: “She will.” / “They won't.”
Yes/No questions start with a helping verb: “Can you count?” / “Is the line straight?”
Wh- questions start with a question word: “What is the distance?” / “How many shells are there?”
Suggestions use Shall: “Shall I measure the size?”
Cause and effect: effect + because + cause. “I checked again because the answer looked wrong.”
You can put the cause first: “Because it was raining, we stayed inside.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “I not will.” / “You can play?” / “I added a number.” (Why?) ✗
Fix: “I won't.” / “Can you play?” / “I added a number because the pattern was not complete.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Won't is will not squeezed together. Flip the subject and the helping verb to ask. Because is the glue between what happened and why.
grammar.practice: Answer with “I will” or “I won't”: A: “Will you help me measure the desk?” B: “______, I'd love to!” | A: “Will you count all the way to a million?” B: “______, that would take too long!” | A: “Will you check the pattern again?” B: “______, good idea.” | ______ is the distance from the door to the window? (asks about a thing) | ______ you measure this shell for me? (Yes/No, about ability) | ______ many bowls are on the table? (asks about number) | ______ we check our pattern again? (a suggestion) | Finish each sentence with a reason using because: We worked as a team ______. | I used multiplication ______. | Amal could not measure the shell ______. Answer key — short answers: 1) I will, I'd love to! 2) I won't, that would take too long! 3) I will, good idea. Question words: 4) What is the distance from the door to the window? 5) Can you measure this shell for me? 6) How many bowls are on the table? 7) Shall we check our pattern again? The three because sentences are open-ended, so there is no single correct answer — check that your reason makes sense, for example: We worked as a team because two heads solve a puzzle faster than one. I used multiplication because it is a fast way to add equal groups. Amal could not measure the shell because it was too small and the line was not straight.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'million' mean in this unit?
quizzes.options: A very big number written 1,000,000, or one thousand thousands. | A unit of length equal to one hundred centimetres. | Going the same way without bending or curving, like a ruler edge. | Splitting a number into equal parts so everyone gets the same.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A very big number written 1,000,000, or one thousand thousands.
quizzes.explanation: One million counts things, so it is a number, not a length.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'measure' mean in this unit?
quizzes.options: A design or sequence of things that repeats in the same order. | How far it is from one place to another place. | To find out the size, length or amount of something. | Taking one number away from another to see what is left.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To find out the size, length or amount of something.
quizzes.explanation: Measure is the action; the others name a pattern, a distance and subtraction.

quizzes.question: What does the word 'pattern' mean in this unit?
quizzes.options: How heavy something is when you put it on the scales. | A design or sequence of things that repeats in the same order. | Something that is true and can be checked or proven. | Adding the same number over and over again to find a total quickly.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A design or sequence of things that repeats in the same order.
quizzes.explanation: A pattern repeats in order, like red, blue, red, blue on the classroom tiles.

quizzes.question: In The Mystery of the Million Shells, how many shells did the teams count in total?
quizzes.explanation: Amal reports 375, and Teacher Yasmin confirms the total is 375 shells.

quizzes.question: Which sentence gives a clear instruction, using an imperative?
quizzes.options: Measure the height of your desk. | She measures the rope every morning. | The desk is one metre high. | Will you measure it tomorrow?
quizzes.correctAnswer: Measure the height of your desk.
quizzes.explanation: An imperative starts with the verb and gives the order straight away.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses 'have got' correctly for one person?
quizzes.options: They has got a metre stick. | We has got ten bowls. | She has got a new ruler. | He have got a bicycle.
quizzes.correctAnswer: She has got a new ruler.
quizzes.explanation: He, she and it take has got, but we and they take have got.

quizzes.question: Which sentence explains a reason with 'because'?
quizzes.options: I used multiplication today. | I used multiplication because it is faster than adding. | Multiplication and addition are both useful maths operations. | Use multiplication now.
quizzes.correctAnswer: I used multiplication because it is faster than adding.
quizzes.explanation: Because joins the effect to its cause, so it tells us why.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from A Pattern Poem: “Five, six, shapes and sticks, _____ and round, patterns found!”
quizzes.explanation: The poem sets straight lines against round ones, so Straight completes the rhyme.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from Maths Is Everywhere: “When Amal helps her mother at the market, she uses _____ to add the prices.”
quizzes.explanation: Adding prices together is addition, which is why the text names that operation.

quizzes.question: In The Measuring Challenge, which tool may the class use?
quizzes.options: A pair of scissors | A colour pencil | A metre stick | A shopping basket
quizzes.explanation: The speaker names a metre stick before telling the class to begin.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Numbers, Shapes, and Measurement" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 7-8 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'number' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Read and say big numbers, up to one million.
Use the maths words addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
Measure the size, height, weight and distance of things around you.
Talk about straight lines and repeating patterns.
Give clear instructions using imperatives, such as “Measure the height.”
Say what you own with have got, and what you can do with can and can't.
Talk about the future with will, and explain reasons using because.

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Numbers and Number Words, Maths Operations, Measurement Words, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Present Simple and Imperatives" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "The Mystery of the Million Shells" together, and enjoy "The Measuring Challenge" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1 — Match the Maths Word" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”
